📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — pick the process model from the project

WORKED EXAMPLE — three projects, three models
• Fixed government contract, complete spec, formal sign-offs → Waterfall (phases once, in order).
• Startup product, requirements change weekly, ship every sprint → Agile/Scrum (short cycles, feedback).
• Huge safety-critical system, management demands explicit risk analysis each cycle → Spiral (its fingerprint).
The decision inputs are always the same three: requirement stability, delivery cadence, and risk tolerance. Cite them and the model choice justifies itself.
⚠️ THE MODEL SETS *WHEN QA HAPPENS*
Waterfall concentrates testing late (defects found late are costliest); Agile bakes testing into every sprint. That link is why a QA course starts with process models.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Software does not just appear. It moves through phases — planning, design, building, testing, releasing, maintaining — and each phase has its own work products and risks. Understanding the SDLC means you can spot where a project is, where it is headed, and where things tend to break.

Core concepts

1. The seven canonical phases. Planning, requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance. Every methodology — Waterfall, Agile, DevOps — rearranges or compresses these phases but does not skip them. They define the lifecycle of every successful piece of software.

2. Planning sets the frame. Scope, resources, schedule, feasibility. The output is a project charter or vision document. Skipping planning is the cheapest way to fail; teams that 'just start coding' typically rebuild major pieces twice.

3. Requirements separate problem from solution. Requirements describe WHAT the system must do, not HOW. Functional requirements describe behaviors ('the system shall send a confirmation email'); non-functional requirements describe quality attributes ('confirmation must arrive within 60 seconds').

4. Design bridges requirements and code. Architecture defines components and their interactions. Detailed design specifies interfaces, data structures, and algorithms. Good design is reviewable on paper before any code is written; bad design surfaces as expensive late-cycle rework.

5. Testing is woven throughout. Modern SDLC integrates testing into every phase: requirements get reviewed, designs get inspected, code gets unit-tested, integrations get tested, and finally the system gets validated against requirements. Testing is no longer 'the last phase before release.'

6. Deployment and maintenance. Deployment moves the software into users' hands. Maintenance — bug fixes, security patches, performance improvements, feature additions — typically consumes 60-80% of a software product's total lifecycle cost.

7. Iteration is the modern norm. Pure sequential SDLC is rare today. Most teams iterate: short cycles touching multiple phases, with planning, design, code, test, deploy happening continuously rather than once. The phases still exist; they just overlap and repeat.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Treating 'planning' as paperwork to skip — early ambiguity becomes expensive late.
  • Writing requirements that contain implementation details ('use a Postgres database') rather than behavior.
  • Pushing testing entirely to the end of the cycle, where defects are 10-100x more expensive to fix.
  • Ignoring the maintenance phase during planning — operations and bug-fix capacity must be budgeted.

Quick recap

The SDLC is a model of how software actually gets built and supported. Whether your team uses Waterfall, Scrum, or Kanban, the underlying phases are the same — what changes is how often you cycle through them and how much they overlap.

Glossary

SDLC
Software Development Life Cycle — the phases through which software is conceived, built, used, and retired.
Functional requirement
A statement of WHAT the system must do (a behavior or feature).
Non-functional requirement
A quality attribute — performance, security, usability, scalability.
Iterative development
Repeating short cycles of plan-design-build-test-release rather than one long sequence.
Maintenance
Ongoing fixes, patches, performance work, and small feature additions after initial release.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Different process models suit different projects. Waterfall works when requirements are stable; Agile thrives on change; DevOps merges development and operations to ship faster and more reliably. The wrong choice creates predictable, painful failures — Agile on a hardware project, Waterfall on a startup, no DevOps on a cloud deployment.

Core concepts

1. Waterfall: sequential and predictable. Each phase finishes before the next starts. Heavy upfront documentation. Best when requirements are truly stable (regulated industries, hardware, government contracts) and changes are expensive once construction starts. Risky when requirements evolve mid-project.

2. Agile: iterative and adaptive. Defined by the Agile Manifesto's four values: individuals/interactions over processes/tools, working software over documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation, responding to change over following a plan. Iterative cycles deliver working software early and often.

3. Scrum: the most common Agile framework. Time-boxed sprints (typically 2 weeks). Three roles: Product Owner (backlog), Scrum Master (process), Development Team (delivery). Five events: sprint planning, daily standup, sprint review, retrospective, the sprint itself. Empirical control via transparency, inspection, adaptation.

4. Kanban: continuous flow with WIP limits. No sprints. A visual board with columns (Backlog, In Progress, In Review, Done) and explicit limits on Work-in-Progress. Pull-based: work moves only when capacity opens downstream. Best for support, ops, and steady-state product work.

5. DevOps: dev plus ops, automated and integrated. Combines development and operations through automation: version control, automated build/test, infrastructure as code, monitoring, and rapid feedback. Reduces deployment risk and shortens lead time from idea to production from months to hours.

6. CI/CD: the technical backbone of DevOps. Continuous Integration: every commit triggers automated build and tests. Continuous Delivery: code is always in a deployable state. Continuous Deployment: every passing change goes to production automatically. Each level reduces release risk further.

7. Picking the right model. Stable requirements, regulated environment → Waterfall or hybrid. Evolving requirements, frequent customer feedback → Scrum. Continuous flow of unrelated work → Kanban. Cloud product needing fast safe deployments → DevOps overlay on whichever flavor of Agile.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Calling something 'Agile' but still requiring full upfront requirements — that is just slow Waterfall.
  • Choosing Scrum for individual contributor work that has no real backlog — Kanban fits better.
  • Adopting DevOps tools without the cultural shift — automation cannot fix a 'us vs them' team dynamic.
  • Treating CI/CD as a single project to 'finish' rather than ongoing investment in build, test, and observability.

Quick recap

Process models are tools, not religions. Waterfall handles stable, regulated work; Agile handles uncertainty; DevOps handles cloud-scale deployment. Most modern teams blend Scrum or Kanban with DevOps practices.

Glossary

Waterfall
Sequential model where each phase completes before the next begins.
Sprint
A time-boxed iteration in Scrum, typically 1-4 weeks, ending in a potentially shippable increment.
WIP limit
An upper bound on items in a Kanban column, preventing overload.
CI/CD
Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery (or Deployment) — automated build/test/release pipeline.
DevOps
A culture and toolset that integrates development and operations through automation and shared accountability.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — QA at every phase, one defect caught four ways

WORKED EXAMPLE — the missing-requirement bug
Requirement omits “max 3 login attempts.” Where could QA catch it?
• Requirements review (cheapest): a checklist question — “are security limits specified?” — catches it before any code.
• Design review: the auth-flow diagram shows no lockout path.
• Testing: a negative test (“4th bad login”) fails… if someone thought to write it.
• Production (costliest): a brute-force incident.
The exam point: defect cost grows ~10× per phase it survives — so QA is a whole-lifecycle activity (reviews, static analysis, tests), not a phase at the end.
⚠️ QA ≠ TESTING
Testing is one QA activity. QA also includes reviews, standards, audits, and process improvement — “prevention over detection” is the graded phrase.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Quality assurance is not a phase at the end — it is an attitude and set of practices applied throughout the lifecycle. Modern QA shapes requirements, reviews designs, automates tests, and partners with operations. Understanding where QA contributes at each phase is what separates a tester from a quality engineer.

Core concepts

1. QA in planning and requirements. Quality engineers participate in requirements review to flag ambiguity and untestability. A requirement that cannot be tested is not a requirement — it is a wish. Catching this in the requirements phase is 100x cheaper than catching it after release.

2. QA in design. Design reviews surface testability issues: hidden state, untestable side effects, tight coupling that prevents mocking. QA also designs the test strategy in parallel with the system architecture, ensuring test environments and data are planned, not improvised.

3. QA during implementation. Developers write unit tests; QA writes integration and system tests, often in parallel with the code. Test automation frameworks are built early so they grow with the codebase rather than being bolted on at the end.

4. QA during testing phases. Unit testing (developer-driven), integration testing, system testing, regression testing, performance testing, security testing, usability testing, acceptance testing. QA orchestrates this pyramid of activities and reports on coverage and defect trends.

5. QA at deployment and beyond. Smoke tests in production, monitoring for quality regressions, gathering user feedback, triaging bug reports. Modern QA owns observability dashboards and incident triage as much as pre-release testing.

6. Shift-left vs shift-right. Shift-left: move testing earlier (requirements review, unit tests, design inspection). Shift-right: extend testing into production (canary releases, A/B tests, observability). Modern teams do both — quality is verified before AND after release.

7. Quality is a team responsibility. QA cannot 'inspect quality in' to bad work. Developers, designers, PMs, and operations all contribute to quality. QA's job is to design the system that makes quality visible, not to be the sole gatekeeper.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Treating QA as a 'check at the end' rather than a continuous activity throughout the lifecycle.
  • Writing test cases only after code is complete — too late to influence design.
  • Assuming developers will test their own code thoroughly without explicit unit-test requirements.
  • Forgetting non-functional testing (performance, security) until the day before release.

Quick recap

Quality assurance touches every SDLC phase. The earlier QA gets involved, the cheaper defects are to prevent. Modern QA is a partner across requirements, design, code, test, and operations — not a gate at the end.

Glossary

Quality Assurance (QA)
Activities that ensure software meets quality standards across the lifecycle.
Test strategy
High-level approach defining what kinds of testing will happen, by whom, and at what depth.
Shift-left testing
Moving QA activities earlier in the lifecycle (requirements review, design inspection, unit tests).
Shift-right testing
Extending QA into production (monitoring, canaries, A/B tests, real-user metrics).
Smoke test
A quick post-deployment sanity check verifying the system is up and core flows work.

Cost curve: the cost of fixing a defect INCREASES the later it is found — cheapest in requirements, most expensive in production — which is why QA belongs in every phase, not just the end. Verification asks “did we build the product RIGHT?” (matches the spec); validation asks “did we build the RIGHT product?” (meets real user needs). QA independence: testers report separately from developers so schedule pressure cannot silence findings — independent judgment combined with daily collaboration.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — from business need to business requirement

WORKED EXAMPLE — the pet-store expansion
Business case: “Phone orders cost $8 each to process; competitors take orders online.”
• Business requirement (the WHY, outcome-level): “Reduce order-processing cost 60% by enabling customer self-service ordering within 12 months.”
• NOT a business requirement: “the checkout button shall be blue” (design) or “the system shall store orders in MySQL” (implementation).
A business case pairs the requirement with costs, benefits, and risks so leadership can decide. Business → functional → design is a strict ladder: each level answers WHY → WHAT → HOW.
⚠️ MEASURABLE OR IT ISN’T A REQUIREMENT
“Improve ordering” fails; “reduce cost 60% in 12 months” passes — a target and a deadline make success testable. Exams reward the measurable phrasing every time.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Software is built to serve a business goal. The business case answers 'why are we doing this?' in dollar terms, and the business requirements translate that into concrete capabilities. Skip these and you ship features that nobody asked for, in projects that nobody can justify.

Core concepts

1. Business case anatomy. A business case typically contains: problem statement, proposed solution, expected benefits (revenue, cost savings, risk reduction), estimated cost, timeline, and risks. It justifies the investment to the funding stakeholder before any work starts.

2. Business requirements vs functional requirements. Business requirements describe outcomes the business needs ('reduce checkout abandonment by 20%'). Functional requirements describe what the software does ('display a single-page checkout'). One business requirement typically generates many functional requirements.

3. Stakeholders and their goals. Stakeholder analysis maps who cares about the project: end users, product owners, executives, regulators, support teams, ops teams. Each has goals that may conflict; the business case must reconcile them.

4. Cost-benefit and ROI. Quantifying expected return on investment helps prioritize. Hard benefits (revenue, savings) and soft benefits (brand, employee experience) both count, but soft benefits need extra rigor in measurement.

5. Success criteria. Measurable, time-bound conditions that define 'this project worked.' Without them, the team cannot recognize success or failure. Vague goals like 'improve user experience' fail this test; 'reduce average task time from 3 minutes to under 1 minute' passes it.

6. The 'why' behind the project. A great business case tells a story: what problem exists, who is hurt by it, what solution is proposed, why this is the right time, and what it will cost. Engineers who understand the why make better technical tradeoffs throughout.

7. When the business case must be revisited. Major scope changes, market shifts, regulatory changes, technology pivots, or learnings from early iterations. A locked-in business case ignored despite changing reality is one of the most common project failure patterns.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Writing a business case full of buzzwords with no measurable outcomes.
  • Skipping stakeholder analysis and discovering at launch that you ignored regulators or operations.
  • Confusing solution-language ('build a mobile app') with problem-language ('field staff cannot access records remotely').
  • Failing to revisit the business case when project assumptions change.

Quick recap

The business case is the project's reason for existing. It states the problem, proposes a solution, estimates costs and benefits, and defines what success looks like. Business requirements derived from it set the stage for everything else.

Glossary

Business case
The justification document explaining why a project should be funded and pursued.
Stakeholder
Anyone with an interest in or impact from the project (users, sponsors, regulators, etc.).
ROI (Return on Investment)
Ratio of project benefit to project cost, often expressed as a percentage or payback period.
Success criteria
Specific, measurable, time-bound conditions for declaring a project successful.

📖 Worked example — writing a testable functional requirement

WORKED EXAMPLE — sharpen it until it’s testable
• ❌ “The system should handle logins well.” — vague, untestable.
• ✅ “The system shall lock an account for 15 minutes after 3 consecutive failed login attempts and display message MSG-401.”
Why it passes: one behavior, a trigger (3 failures), an observable outcome (lockout + message), numbers you can verify. A tester can derive test cases directly: 2 failures → no lock; 3 → locked; retry at 14 min → still locked; 16 min → unlocked. FUNCTIONAL = what the system DOES (behaviors); each “shall” statement maps to test cases one-to-one.
⚠️ ONE REQUIREMENT, ONE BEHAVIOR
“The system shall lock accounts AND email the admin AND log the event” hides three requirements — split them so each can pass or fail independently. Compound “shall” statements are the classic review finding.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Functional requirements are the contract between the business and the engineering team. They define what the software must do — feature by feature, behavior by behavior. Get them right and design becomes possible; get them wrong and you build the wrong thing efficiently.

Core concepts

1. Definition of a functional requirement. A statement of what the system must do — an action it performs, an input it accepts, an output it produces, a rule it enforces. Each requirement should be atomic (one behavior per requirement) and testable (you can verify whether it is met).

2. Common formats. Plain-language shall statements ('The system shall send a confirmation email upon order placement'). User stories ('As a buyer, I want a confirmation email so I know my order was received'). Use cases (actor + system + flow). Each format has strengths; teams pick one and stick with it.

3. Acceptance criteria. The pass/fail conditions that close out a requirement. A user story is not done until its acceptance criteria are met. Common formats: given/when/then (Gherkin), checklists, scenarios with expected outcomes.

4. Quality attributes of a good requirement. The classic acronym is SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. INVEST adds Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable for stories. The common thread: clear, testable, scoped.

5. Traceability. Each functional requirement should trace to a business requirement (why it exists) and forward to the design, code, and test cases that satisfy it. A requirements traceability matrix (RTM) makes this explicit.

6. Prioritization. Not every requirement is equal. MoSCoW (Must, Should, Could, Won't) is a common framework. Kano analysis distinguishes basic, performance, and delight features. Without prioritization, every feature feels equally critical and the project drowns.

7. Refinement is ongoing. Requirements are rarely complete on day one. Backlog refinement, design discoveries, and customer feedback all surface new requirements. The discipline is to keep them documented and testable rather than letting them live only in someone's head.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Vague requirements ('the system should be user-friendly') that cannot be tested.
  • Combining multiple behaviors into one requirement, making it impossible to mark partially done.
  • Specifying solution rather than need ('use Redis cache') instead of intent ('responses must be served in under 200ms').
  • Skipping acceptance criteria — requirements without them tend to be 'done' when the developer says so, not when the system actually meets the need.

Quick recap

Functional requirements are atomic, testable statements of system behavior. They are written in a consistent format, traced to business goals, prioritized, and equipped with acceptance criteria. They are also revisited as the project learns.

Glossary

Functional requirement
A statement of what the system must do — a specific behavior or feature.
User story
Short requirement format: 'As a [user], I want [feature] so that [benefit]'.
Acceptance criteria
Conditions that must be true for a requirement to be considered complete.
RTM (Requirements Traceability Matrix)
A document mapping each requirement to its source, design, code, and tests.
MoSCoW
Prioritization scheme: Must / Should / Could / Won't have.

A use case describes how an actor interacts with the system to achieve a goal — named from the actor’s perspective: examples include Search for product, Place order, Reset password. In the Endothon-style scenarios, identify each company’s actors first, then write one use case per goal — the diagram falls out of that list.

Newer companies: when a company has little operating history, base projections on a mix of the historical data that exists plus clearly-labeled forecasted estimates — and state the assumptions.

📊 FIGURE — what each modal verb commits you to
🎯 EXAM TIP
"Shall" indicates mandatory functionality. The distinction is contractual, not stylistic: "shall" creates a requirement that must be verified, "should" is a recommendation, and "may" is optional. A requirement written with "should" cannot be failed at acceptance.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — non-functional requirements, quantified

WORKED EXAMPLE — the same app, its NFR sheet
• Performance: “95% of searches return in under 2 seconds at 1,000 concurrent users.”
• Availability: “99.9% uptime monthly (≤ 43 min downtime).”
• Security: “passwords stored salted-and-hashed; all traffic TLS.”
• Usability: “a new user completes checkout in under 3 minutes without help.”
• Scalability/maintainability/portability round out the -ilities.
Functional = what it does; non-functional = HOW WELL it does it. NFRs still need numbers — that’s what makes them testable (load tests, uptime monitors, usability sessions).
⚠️ “FAST” IS NOT A REQUIREMENT
Every NFR on the exam should carry a metric + threshold + condition. If an option lacks numbers, it’s the wrong answer to “which is well-formed?”
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Non-functional requirements (NFRs) define how well the system does what it does. They cover speed, reliability, security, usability, and more. Functional bugs anger users; NFR failures lose customers — a slow, insecure, or unreliable product fails even when every feature works.

Core concepts

1. What NFRs cover. Quality attributes the system must possess: performance (speed, throughput), scalability (handling growth), reliability (uptime, mean time between failures), availability, security, maintainability, portability, usability, accessibility. Sometimes called 'ilities' for the way many of them end.

2. Performance specifics. Throughput (requests per second), latency (response time), resource utilization. Each must be specified with both a target and a measurement context — 'page loads in under 1 second on a 4G connection at p95'.

3. Security as an NFR family. Confidentiality (data not exposed to unauthorized parties), integrity (data not modified inappropriately), availability (data accessible when needed), authentication, authorization, audit. Modern teams treat security as engineering, not paperwork.

4. Usability and accessibility. Usability is how easily users can accomplish goals. Accessibility ensures the product works for people with disabilities — screen readers, keyboard navigation, color contrast. Both have measurable criteria (WCAG levels, task completion rates).

5. Maintainability and supportability. Code that future engineers can understand, change safely, and operate. Includes documentation, observability, error handling, and modular design. Often invisible until it is missing, when it dominates total cost of ownership.

6. Trade-offs are unavoidable. Performance often costs simplicity. Security often costs convenience. Reliability costs money. NFRs force tradeoffs to be explicit rather than discovered late. The architecture's job is largely to balance NFRs.

7. Testability of NFRs. Each NFR must have a measurable target and an agreed measurement method. 'The system must be fast' is not testable; 'p95 latency under 200ms with 1000 concurrent users measured via JMeter against the staging environment' is.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Vague NFRs ('the system must be reliable') that cannot drive design decisions.
  • Ignoring NFRs until late — by then, retrofitting performance, security, or accessibility is expensive.
  • Specifying conflicting NFRs without resolving the trade-off ('99.999% uptime AND under $10K/month infrastructure').
  • Treating accessibility as an extra rather than a core requirement — it is often a legal requirement and always a quality requirement.

Quick recap

NFRs describe the qualities of the system: how fast, how secure, how reliable, how usable. They drive architecture more than functional requirements do, force explicit trade-offs, and must be specified with measurable targets and verification methods.

Glossary

Non-functional requirement (NFR)
A quality attribute of the system rather than a feature — speed, security, etc.
Latency
Time elapsed between a request and its response.
Throughput
Number of requests or transactions processed per unit time.
Availability
Percentage of time the system is operational and accessible.
WCAG
Web Content Accessibility Guidelines — the standard for web accessibility.

📖 Worked example — drawing the scope line

WORKED EXAMPLE — release 1 of the ordering site
In scope: browse catalog, cart, credit-card checkout, order-status email.
Out of scope (this release): loyalty points, gift cards, international shipping, mobile app.

Writing the OUT list is as important as the IN list: it prevents scope creep (“while you’re at it, add gift cards”) and sets stakeholder expectations in writing. Change control then handles additions deliberately: impact-analyze → approve/reject → re-baseline schedule and budget.
⚠️ UNSTATED = ASSUMED IN
If international shipping isn’t explicitly excluded, someone will assume it’s included — and its absence becomes a “defect” at acceptance. Explicit exclusions are cheap insurance; that’s the graded rationale.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Scope is what the project will and will not do. Vague scope is the leading cause of late, over-budget, frustrated software projects. Explicit scope statements stop arguments months later about whether something was 'always' part of the project.

Core concepts

1. What the scope statement contains. A list of in-scope features, capabilities, integrations, and platforms. Equally important: a list of explicitly out-of-scope items so stakeholders cannot later claim those were assumed. Plus assumptions, dependencies, and constraints.

2. Out-of-scope is as important as in-scope. Saying what you will NOT build prevents scope creep. 'Mobile app' is in scope; 'native iOS and Android with offline sync' is out of scope and will be a future phase. Documenting this prevents future arguments.

3. Scope creep vs scope evolution. Creep: features added over time without rebalancing budget or schedule. Evolution: planned, agreed-upon scope changes via a change-control process. Creep kills projects; evolution is normal.

4. The change control process. Any in-flight change to scope goes through a defined process: who proposes, who reviews, who decides, what gets adjusted (timeline, budget, other features). Without this, scope drifts and accountability evaporates.

5. Assumptions and dependencies. Assumptions: things you believe to be true but have not verified ('the legacy API will remain stable'). Dependencies: things outside your team's control that affect the project ('the data team will deliver the dataset by Q3'). Both are project risks if wrong.

6. Constraints. Hard limits that bound the solution: budget, timeline, technology stack, regulatory rules, headcount. Constraints often determine scope as much as desired features do.

7. Documenting scope visibly. Scope lives in the project charter, the PRD, the SOW (Statement of Work) for contractors. It is reviewed and signed off by stakeholders. Re-baselined when major changes occur.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Listing only in-scope items without an out-of-scope list — leaves implicit features that 'everyone assumed' would be there.
  • Letting scope changes happen verbally with no documented impact on schedule or budget.
  • Treating dependencies as someone else's problem rather than tracking them as project risks.
  • Failing to revisit scope when constraints (budget, timeline) change.

Quick recap

Scope sets the boundaries of the project. Explicit in-scope and out-of-scope lists, plus assumptions, dependencies, and constraints, anchor stakeholder expectations. A change-control process keeps the project from drifting.

Glossary

Scope
The full set of features, capabilities, and outcomes the project will deliver.
Out-of-scope
Items explicitly NOT included in the project — equally important to document.
Scope creep
Uncontrolled expansion of scope without rebalancing time, cost, or other features.
Change control
The defined process for evaluating and approving scope changes mid-project.
Statement of Work (SOW)
A document defining scope, deliverables, timeline, and acceptance for contracted work.
📊 FIGURE — keeping scope tied to the business need
🎯 EXAM TIP
Scope should align with business requirements. The practical form of that rule is traceability: every item in scope points at a stated requirement, and anything that cannot be traced is either scope creep or gold plating.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — SOLID, one violation fixed

WORKED EXAMPLE — the god class, refactored
OrderManager validates orders, charges cards, prints labels, AND emails receipts — four reasons to change = a Single Responsibility violation.
Refactor: OrderValidator, PaymentProcessor, ShippingLabeler, ReceiptMailer — each with ONE reason to change; OrderManager just coordinates.

The other four, one line each: Open/closed — extend via new classes, don’t edit stable ones (add PayPal by adding a class, not a switch case). Liskov — a subclass must work anywhere its parent does. Interface segregation — many small interfaces beat one fat one. Dependency inversion — depend on abstractions (interfaces), not concrete classes.
⚠️ SPOT THE PRINCIPLE BY SYMPTOM
“Class changes for many reasons” → SRP. “Must edit a switch to add a type” → OCP. “Subclass breaks parent’s contract” → LSP. “Forced to implement unused methods” → ISP. “High-level code news up low-level classes” → DIP.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Bad design rots over time — small additions create exponential complexity until the codebase is too risky to change. Design principles are the heuristics that resist rot. SOLID is the five-letter shorthand every senior developer should be able to discuss fluently.

Core concepts

1. Single Responsibility Principle (S). A class or module should have one reason to change. If billing logic and PDF generation live in the same class, both will tug at it. Splitting them isolates change. Most engineers err by combining too much into one class, not too little.

2. Open/Closed Principle (O). Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. Add new behavior by writing new code (a subclass, a strategy implementation, a plugin), not by editing existing code. Achieved through abstraction and polymorphism.

3. Liskov Substitution Principle (L). Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without breaking the program. If Square inherits from Rectangle but breaks code that sets width and height independently, the inheritance is wrong. Inheritance must preserve behavior contracts, not just signatures.

4. Interface Segregation Principle (I). Clients should not depend on methods they do not use. Many small focused interfaces beat one large catch-all. Reduces coupling and prevents 'fat interface' bloat where every implementer must stub methods irrelevant to its actual job.

5. Dependency Inversion Principle (D). High-level modules depend on abstractions, not on concrete low-level modules. The business logic talks to a Repository interface; the database-specific implementation plugs in behind it. Enables testing, swapping implementations, and inverting traditional layered dependencies.

6. Beyond SOLID: DRY, KISS, YAGNI. DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) — extract repeated logic. KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid) — prefer simple solutions over clever ones. YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It) — do not build for hypothetical future needs that may never come.

7. Principles guide, not dictate. SOLID is not a religion. Sometimes a small script's right answer violates several principles. The principles are most valuable in code that will live and grow for years, where the cost of bad design compounds.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Over-applying SRP into a maze of one-method classes that obscure rather than clarify.
  • Inheritance that violates LSP — Square-from-Rectangle is the classic example.
  • Designing for abstract reuse before any second use exists — premature abstraction is as bad as no abstraction.
  • Treating SOLID as checkboxes rather than as a way of thinking about change risk.

Quick recap

SOLID is five principles for designing classes and modules that survive change: one responsibility, extend rather than modify, preserve substitution contracts, narrow interfaces, depend on abstractions. Combined with DRY, KISS, and YAGNI, they form the working vocabulary of object-oriented design.

Glossary

SOLID
Acronym for five OO design principles: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, Dependency Inversion.
Coupling
Degree of interdependence between modules. Lower coupling = easier change.
Cohesion
Degree to which a module's elements belong together. Higher cohesion = clearer responsibility.
DRY
Don't Repeat Yourself — encapsulate repeated logic.
YAGNI

📖 Worked example — recognize the pattern from the design problem

WORKED EXAMPLE — four problems, four patterns
• “Exactly one configuration object shared app-wide” → Singleton.
• “Create the right payment handler per country without callers knowing the class” → Factory.
• “When inventory changes, notify dashboard, email, and audit log” → Observer.
• “Legacy tax library’s interface doesn’t match our new API” → Adapter.
Patterns are named solutions to recurring design problems — the exam gives the problem in plain words and expects the name. Group them: creational (Singleton, Factory, Builder), structural (Adapter, Facade, Decorator), behavioral (Observer, Strategy, Command).
⚠️ PATTERNS ARE VOCABULARY, NOT REQUIREMENTS
“Use more patterns” is never the goal; matching the RIGHT pattern to a stated problem is. Forcing patterns where none fit is itself a design smell (the graded caution).
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Design patterns are named solutions to recurring problems. They give engineers a shared vocabulary — saying 'use a Strategy here' is faster and clearer than describing the structure from scratch. Knowing patterns lets you recognize them in unfamiliar code and apply them where they fit.

Core concepts

1. Three pattern categories. Creational: how objects are made (Singleton, Factory, Builder, Prototype, Abstract Factory). Structural: how objects compose (Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy, Composite). Behavioral: how objects interact (Strategy, Observer, Command, Iterator, State, Template Method).

2. Singleton: one instance ever. Ensures a class has only one instance and provides global access. Useful for shared resources like loggers or connection pools, but often overused — global state hurts testability. Use sparingly and prefer dependency injection when possible.

3. Factory: encapsulate object creation. Hides the 'new' call behind a method or class so callers do not couple themselves to specific concrete types. Especially useful when the right type to create depends on input or configuration. Abstract Factory groups families of related products.

4. Strategy: interchangeable algorithms. Encapsulates a family of algorithms behind a common interface and makes them interchangeable at runtime. Pricing strategies, sort orders, validation rules — anything where 'how to do X' might vary. Replaces big if/else chains keyed on type.

5. Observer: publish-subscribe. Defines a one-to-many dependency: when the subject changes state, observers are notified automatically. Backbone of GUI event systems, reactive programming, and event-driven architectures.

6. Decorator: layered behavior. Adds responsibilities to an object dynamically without subclassing. Wrapping a stream with buffering, then encryption, then compression is a classic example. Each decorator implements the same interface as the wrapped object.

7. Pattern overuse is real. Applying patterns where they do not fit creates 'pattern soup' — code that is harder to understand than the simple solution it replaced. The mature mindset is: recognize the problem first, choose pattern only if it actually simplifies.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Forcing a pattern where a simple function or class would do.
  • Singleton-everywhere for globals you should be passing as parameters.
  • Implementing patterns by rote without understanding the problem they solve.
  • Stacking decorators or factories so deep that following the code requires a map.

Quick recap

Design patterns are reusable solutions to common design problems, grouped into creational, structural, and behavioral families. Used well, they accelerate communication and design; used reflexively, they obscure simple solutions. Apply them when the problem matches the pattern, not because the pattern is famous.

Glossary

Design pattern
A named, reusable solution to a recurring software design problem.
Creational pattern
A pattern dealing with object creation (e.g., Factory, Singleton).
Structural pattern
A pattern dealing with object composition (e.g., Adapter, Decorator).
Behavioral pattern
A pattern dealing with object interaction (e.g., Strategy, Observer).
Gang of Four (GoF)
The four authors of the seminal 1994 book that catalogued 23 classic design patterns.
📊 FIGURE — Model-View-Controller
🎯 EXAM TIP
MVC is Model-View-Controller. The benefit to state is separation of concerns: business logic lives in the model and can be tested with no interface present, so the presentation can be replaced without disturbing the rules.

📖 Worked example — choose the architecture style

WORKED EXAMPLE — same store, three architectures
• Monolithic: one deployable with UI + logic + data layers inside. Simple to build/deploy; scaling and team autonomy suffer as it grows.
• Client-server / N-tier: presentation → application → database tiers; each scales and updates separately.
• Microservices: catalog, cart, payment as independent services with their own databases, talking via APIs — independent deploys and scaling, at the price of distributed-system complexity.
Choose by: team size, scaling needs, deployment cadence. Small team, one product → monolith first. Many teams shipping independently at scale → microservices.
⚠️ MICROSERVICES AREN’T FREE
Network failures, distributed data consistency, and operational overhead come with the style. “When is a monolith the RIGHT answer?” — small team, early product — is a real exam question.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Architecture styles are the macro-level design decisions that shape every other choice — how the system is partitioned, how parts communicate, what scaling and failure look like. The wrong style for the problem becomes a chronic cost; the right style accelerates the team for years.

Core concepts

1. Monolith: everything in one deployable. A single application containing all features, deployed as one unit. Simplest to build, test, and deploy at small scale. Becomes painful when team size grows past ~30 engineers or when parts have very different scaling needs.

2. Layered (n-tier) architecture. Stacked layers (presentation, business logic, data access, database) where each layer only talks to the layer below. Common in classic enterprise applications. Easy to reason about; sometimes too rigid when cross-cutting concerns appear.

3. Microservices: many small deployables. The system is split into independent services, each owning its data, deployed and scaled separately. Enables team autonomy and independent scaling. Costs: operational complexity, distributed-system bugs, harder local testing. Worth it at scale; overkill at small.

4. Event-driven architecture. Services communicate through events rather than direct calls. Loose coupling, natural async, good for spiky load. But debugging and consistency are harder; events can be lost or processed out of order.

5. Service-oriented architecture (SOA). Older sibling of microservices, often centered on enterprise service buses and shared schemas. More heavyweight than microservices; less common in greenfield work today but still common in enterprise.

6. Serverless / FaaS. Functions deploy and scale on demand, billed per invocation. Removes server management; introduces cold starts, vendor lock-in, and complex local testing. Great for spiky, simple workloads; awkward for stateful or latency-critical paths.

7. Choosing a style. Start simple. A monolith with a clean modular interior carries most teams to several million users. Move to microservices when team size, deployment cadence, or scaling needs justify the operational cost — not because microservices are fashionable.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Adopting microservices because they are trendy, before the team has the operational maturity to run them.
  • Building a 'distributed monolith' — services that all must deploy together, getting all the costs of microservices and none of the benefits.
  • Mixing event-driven and synchronous patterns inconsistently, making system behavior hard to predict.
  • Choosing serverless for everything, then suffering on long-running, stateful, or latency-sensitive workloads.

Quick recap

Architecture styles are tradeoffs, not rankings. Monoliths are simple; microservices buy team autonomy at high operational cost; event-driven decouples but complicates debugging; serverless scales without management but adds vendor coupling. Pick by problem, team size, and team operational maturity.

Glossary

Monolith
A single deployable application containing all of the system's functionality.
Microservice
An independently deployable service owning one capability and its own data.
Event-driven architecture
A style where components communicate by emitting and reacting to events.
Serverless / FaaS
Functions-as-a-service — managed runtime that scales per invocation.
Distributed monolith
Anti-pattern: services split physically but coupled logically, requiring lockstep deployment.
📊 FIGURE — ports and adapters
🎯 EXAM TIP
Hexagonal architecture is ports and adapters. The domain defines the interfaces (ports) it needs in its own vocabulary, and infrastructure supplies implementations (adapters). Because all dependencies point inward, the database, the web framework and the message queue are all replaceable details.

📖 Worked example — designing a component interface

WORKED EXAMPLE — the InventoryService contract
InventoryService (interface)
  reserve(itemId, qty) → ReservationResult   // success | insufficient
  release(reservationId) → void
  available(itemId) → int
The interface states WHAT, hides HOW (database? cache? third-party?). Callers couple to the contract, so the implementation can change freely — that’s low coupling. Inside, everything about inventory lives together — high cohesion. Good component design = high cohesion within, low coupling between, contracts at the seams.
⚠️ COHESION HIGH, COUPLING LOW — NEVER THE REVERSE
The exam’s favorite pairing. If modules constantly reach into each other’s internals: high coupling (bad). If one module does unrelated jobs: low cohesion (bad).
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Components are the units of design between 'class' and 'system.' Their interfaces define contracts other components rely on. Sloppy interfaces leak implementation details, create tight coupling, and turn small changes into breaking ones.

Core concepts

1. What a component is. A coherent unit of functionality with a well-defined interface and bounded responsibility. Larger than a class, smaller than a service. A component might be a library, a module, a package, or a logical group of classes.

2. Interface design rules. Interfaces should be minimal (only what callers need), stable (changes must be backward-compatible), explicit (every assumption named), and testable. Documentation lives at the interface level — implementation details are private.

3. Public vs internal. What is public is contractual. What is internal can change at will. Aggressively keeping things internal reduces the surface area you must support and the blast radius of changes. 'Public until proven internal' is the wrong default.

4. Versioning interfaces. Once a component's interface is published to other teams, breaking changes require coordination. Strategies: semantic versioning, deprecation periods, parallel versions during migration. Painful, so good initial design pays compound interest.

5. Cohesion at the component level. A component should do one thing well. If a component handles billing AND user notifications AND PDF generation, it is too broad. Split until each component has one clear responsibility and a name that captures it.

6. Coupling between components. Loose coupling means a change in one component rarely forces changes in another. Achieved by interfaces, dependency injection, events, and avoiding shared mutable state. Tight coupling makes refactoring across components a coordinated nightmare.

7. The 'plug-in' mindset. Design components as if they will be plugged in by someone else — possibly years later, possibly without your help. That mindset produces clear interfaces, good docs, and low coupling. Even if you are the only consumer, it improves the design.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Components with leaky interfaces — exposing internal data structures or implementation details.
  • Treating every public method as a permanent contract when it could be internal.
  • Skipping versioning, then breaking other teams when the interface evolves.
  • Letting components grow until 'one component' covers half the system.

Quick recap

Components are the mid-scale units of software design. Their interfaces are contracts: small, stable, explicit, testable. High cohesion within a component and loose coupling between components are the goals. Versioning matters once an interface is public.

Glossary

Component
A coherent unit of functionality with a defined interface; larger than a class, smaller than a service.
Interface
The published contract by which other code interacts with a component.
Cohesion
Degree to which a component's parts work together toward one purpose.
Coupling
Degree of interdependence between components.
Semantic versioning
Versioning convention: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH where MAJOR signals breaking changes.

📘 Deep dive: designing services & UML

Good service design gives each service ONE clear responsibility: a FiscalYearService computes fiscal-year boundaries and nothing else; a DataValidationService validates input against rules and nothing else. Single-purpose services are testable, reusable, and replaceable. UML — the Unified Modeling Language — is the standard notation for designs: class diagrams show structure and relationships; sequence diagrams show the order of calls between services for a scenario. On design questions, match the service name to its single responsibility.

Two more UML views: a deployment diagram shows where components physically run (servers, devices); an activity diagram shows the movement/flow of a process from start to finish, including decisions and parallel paths.

📖 Worked example — quality metrics, computed

WORKED EXAMPLE — read the release’s health from numbers
Release stats: 10,000 LOC; 40 defects found in testing, 10 found by customers in the first quarter.
• Defect density = 50 / 10 KLOC = 5 defects/KLOC.
• Defect removal efficiency = found-before-release / total = 40/50 = 80% (industry-good is 85%+ — testing needs strengthening).
• MTTF/MTTR track reliability and repair speed; test coverage (% of code exercised by tests) tracks safety net breadth.
Metrics turn “is quality okay?” into trends you can act on — the QA-plan section graders expect.
⚠️ COVERAGE MEASURES EXECUTION, NOT CORRECTNESS
100% coverage with weak assertions proves nothing — code ran, results weren’t checked. Pair coverage with defect metrics; never present it alone as “quality.”
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

What gets measured gets managed. Without metrics, 'quality' is opinion, and arguments about whether the project is on track become political rather than empirical. Good metrics surface trends, expose risks, and reward the right behaviors.

Core concepts

1. Defect-based metrics. Defect density (defects per KLOC), defect leakage (defects found post-release), defect age (time from introduction to fix), reopen rate (fixes that did not actually fix). Each tells a different story about where quality is leaking.

2. Coverage metrics. Code coverage (lines, branches, functions executed by tests), requirements coverage (which requirements have associated tests), test execution coverage (which tests have run recently). Coverage shows breadth, not depth — high coverage with weak assertions still misses bugs.

3. Process metrics. Velocity (story points per sprint), cycle time (time from start to done for a unit of work), lead time (time from request to delivery), throughput (items completed per period). Help diagnose where the team is slow or stuck.

4. Customer-facing metrics. Net Promoter Score (NPS), customer satisfaction (CSAT), task success rate, support tickets per release. Connect engineering output to user experience. Falling NPS after a release is louder than any internal metric.

5. Reliability metrics. Uptime / availability (typically a percentage like 99.95%), mean time between failures (MTBF), mean time to recovery (MTTR), error rate, change failure rate. Especially important for SaaS and operations-heavy products.

6. Choosing a metrics set. Too few metrics: blind spots. Too many: nobody pays attention. Pick a small dashboard (5-10 metrics) covering process, code, defects, and user experience. Review regularly. Replace metrics that no longer drive the right behavior.

7. Metrics drive behavior — choose carefully. Goodhart's Law: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.' Tracking lines of code rewards verbose code. Tracking defect counts incentivizes underreporting. Choose metrics that are hard to game and connect to actual quality.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Tracking lines of code or commits as productivity — easily gamed and uncorrelated with value.
  • Reporting metrics in isolation rather than as trends over time.
  • Confusing high test coverage with high test quality.
  • Letting metrics dashboards get stale until nobody trusts them.

Quick recap

Quality metrics make quality discussable. A balanced set covers code (coverage, complexity), defects (density, leakage), process (velocity, cycle time), and customers (NPS, support load). The metrics you choose change behavior, so choose ones that reward what you actually want.

Glossary

Defect density
Number of defects per unit of code (often per 1000 lines).
Code coverage
Percentage of code exercised by tests.
MTBF
Mean Time Between Failures — average uptime between incidents.
MTTR
Mean Time to Recovery — average time to restore service after an incident.
Goodhart's Law
When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.

📖 Worked example — a test plan’s skeleton, filled in

WORKED EXAMPLE — test plan for the checkout feature
• Scope: cart, payment, confirmation (NOT the admin portal).
• Approach: unit tests per service; integration tests cart↔payment; E2E happy path + top 5 error paths; regression suite nightly.
• Resources & schedule: 2 testers, staging env, weeks 3-4.
• Entry criteria: code complete, unit tests green. Exit criteria: 0 critical defects open, 95% tests passing, coverage ≥ 80%.
• Risks: payment sandbox instability → mock fallback.
The plan answers what/how/who/when/when-do-we-stop BEFORE testing starts — exit criteria are what make “done” objective.
⚠️ EXIT CRITERIA STOP THE ARGUMENTS
Without agreed exit criteria, release day becomes opinion. “What belongs in a test plan?” — scope, approach, resources, schedule, entry/exit criteria, risks — memorize the list.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A test strategy is the multi-quarter direction; a test plan is the per-release tactics. Without them, testing becomes reactive — chasing whatever the loudest stakeholder noticed last. With them, the team allocates effort to the highest-risk, highest-value areas in advance.

Core concepts

1. Strategy vs plan. Strategy is high-level and long-lived: types of testing the org performs, tooling, environments, automation goals, ownership. Plan is project- or release-specific: scope, schedule, resources, exit criteria. Strategy informs plans; plans execute strategy.

2. Test plan contents. Scope (what is in/out), test items (modules, features), testing types (unit, integration, system, performance, security), schedule, environments, data, roles, entry and exit criteria, risks, deliverables.

3. Risk-based testing. Not every feature deserves equal test effort. Prioritize by risk = likelihood of failure × impact of failure. The login flow gets exhaustive testing; the rarely-used admin export gets just enough. Risk-based plans focus effort where it matters.

4. Entry and exit criteria. Entry criteria: prerequisites for starting a test phase (code complete, environment ready, smoke test passing). Exit criteria: conditions for finishing (test cases executed, defect threshold met, blocker count zero). Both prevent fuzzy 'we're done' decisions.

5. Environments and data. Plan which environments will be used (dev, QA, staging, prod-like) and how test data will be obtained and reset. Real data has privacy implications; synthetic data may miss edge cases. Most teams use a mix.

6. Automation strategy. Decide what to automate first (high-value, high-stability paths), what to leave manual (exploratory, usability), how to run automated tests (CI on every commit vs nightly), and how to maintain them. Automation rots without maintenance.

7. Plans are living documents. Test plans evolve as scope, risk, and findings evolve. Keep them current; abandoned plans damage credibility. A short, regularly-updated plan beats a comprehensive one that nobody reads.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Writing a 50-page test plan that no one reads, then doing ad-hoc testing anyway.
  • Equal-effort testing for every feature regardless of risk.
  • Vague exit criteria ('all critical bugs fixed' without defining critical) that allow projects to claim completion despite real issues.
  • Skipping environment and data planning until testing starts and discovering bottlenecks then.

Quick recap

A test strategy sets the long-term approach; test plans drive the work for each release. Both prioritize by risk, define explicit entry and exit criteria, and stay updated. They make the team's testing decisions visible and reviewable rather than ad-hoc.

Glossary

Test strategy
High-level, long-lived approach to testing across the organization.
Test plan
Project- or release-specific document defining scope, schedule, resources, and criteria for testing.
Entry criteria
Conditions that must be met before a test phase can begin.
Exit criteria
Conditions that must be met before a test phase can be considered complete.
Risk-based testing
Allocating test effort proportional to risk = likelihood × impact of failure.

📖 Worked example — a complete test case + boundary data

WORKED EXAMPLE — TC-17: lockout after failed logins
ID: TC-17        Requirement: REQ-authentication-3
Precondition: account exists, unlocked
Steps: 1) enter wrong password ×3   2) attempt correct login
Expected: account locked message MSG-401; correct login rejected
           until 15 minutes elapse
Data: user=test01  passwords=[bad1,bad2,bad3,Correct#1]
Boundary-value data for “3 attempts”: test at 2, 3, and 4 — the edges — not at 1 and 10. Equivalence partitioning: one valid password class, one invalid class; a representative from each. Traceability: every test case cites its requirement, so coverage gaps are visible.
⚠️ EXPECTED RESULT WRITTEN FIRST
A test case without a precise expected result can’t fail — the tester just watches. Steps + data + EXPECTED OUTCOME per case; boundaries at the edges; each case traceable to a requirement.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A test case captures the question 'does the system do X correctly?' in a form that can be executed and verified. Test data provides the concrete inputs. Together they turn vague quality goals into reproducible, repeatable evidence of quality.

Core concepts

1. Anatomy of a good test case. ID and title, preconditions, steps, expected result, actual result, status, traceability to a requirement. Each piece supports a different audience: tester executing, dev debugging, manager reporting.

2. Positive and negative cases. Positive: confirm the system does what it should under normal conditions. Negative: confirm the system handles bad inputs, edge cases, and error conditions gracefully. Most defects live at boundaries and in error paths — negative cases find them.

3. Equivalence partitioning. Group inputs into classes that the system likely treats the same way (e.g., ages 18-64 vs under 18 vs 65+). Test one representative per class. Avoids redundant tests while preserving coverage of behavior space.

4. Boundary value analysis. Test at the edges of equivalence classes (17, 18, 19; 64, 65, 66). Bugs cluster at boundaries because off-by-one errors and threshold checks are common.

5. Test data management. Synthetic data (generated, no privacy issues, may miss edge cases). Anonymized production data (realistic but requires sanitization). Mock data sets for specific scenarios. Plan how data is created, used, and reset between runs.

6. Reusability and maintainability. Test cases get rewritten or thrown away when the UI changes. Reusable cases use stable identifiers, abstract over UI details, and live in version control alongside the code they test. Brittle test cases erode trust in the test suite.

7. Manual vs automated cases. Some cases will be automated (regression candidates, fast-feedback critical paths). Some remain manual (exploratory, hard-to-automate UX flows). Both are legitimate; the question is which deserves automation investment.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Writing only happy-path cases — the bugs are in the unhappy paths.
  • Relying on shared mutable test data across cases — flaky tests when run in different orders.
  • Hardcoding production-like data with PII into test cases (security and compliance risk).
  • Not maintaining test cases as features evolve, leaving stale instructions that no longer match the system.

Quick recap

Test cases are the executable form of quality questions. Good cases include preconditions, steps, expected results, and traceability. Equivalence partitioning and boundary analysis multiply the value per case. Test data must be planned for realism, repeatability, and privacy.

Glossary

Test case
A documented set of preconditions, steps, and expected results to verify a specific behavior.
Equivalence partitioning
Grouping inputs into classes treated equivalently to reduce redundant tests.
Boundary value analysis
Testing at the edges of equivalence classes where bugs cluster.
Test data
The inputs (and reference outputs) used to drive and verify test cases.
Traceability
Linking each test case to the requirement(s) it verifies.

📖 Worked example — one TDD cycle, red to green

WORKED EXAMPLE — building discount logic test-first
RED — write the failing test first:
@Test void tenPercentOffOver100() {
    assertEquals(90.0, Pricing.discounted(100.0), 0.01);
}   // fails: discounted() doesn't exist yet
GREEN — write the least code to pass: return total >= 100 ? total * 0.9 : total;
REFACTOR — clean up names/duplication with the test as a safety net.
Repeat per behavior (boundary at exactly 100, below 100…). The test suite becomes executable documentation and the regression net for every future change.
⚠️ TDD ORDER IS THE ANSWER
Red → green → refactor, test BEFORE code. Any option with “write the code, then the tests” is describing test-after, not TDD. Unit tests: one unit, isolated, fast, repeatable.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Unit tests are the cheapest, fastest, most precise feedback loop developers have. They catch defects at the keystroke rather than the release. Test-Driven Development takes this further, using tests to drive the design itself — code emerges shaped to be testable, modular, and small.

Core concepts

1. What a unit test verifies. A unit test exercises one unit (a function, a method, a class) in isolation, with all dependencies mocked or stubbed. Fast (milliseconds), focused, and deterministic. Should run on every save, every commit, every push.

2. Test structure: AAA. Arrange (set up the inputs and dependencies), Act (call the unit under test), Assert (verify the result). This three-step pattern is universal across languages and frameworks.

3. TDD: red, green, refactor. Write a failing test (red). Write the minimum code to pass it (green). Improve the design without breaking tests (refactor). Repeat. Forces small steps, testable design, and high coverage by construction.

4. Mocking and stubbing. Mocks: objects that record interactions for verification. Stubs: objects that return canned responses. Both isolate the unit from its dependencies. Overuse leads to tests that pass even when production code is broken — mock only what crosses a real boundary.

5. Property-based testing. Generative testing: instead of specifying examples, specify properties that must hold for all inputs (e.g., 'reverse(reverse(x)) === x'). Frameworks generate hundreds of inputs to try to falsify the property. Catches edge cases human-written examples miss.

6. Coverage and its limits. 100% line coverage doesn't mean every behavior is tested — it means every line ran during a test. Mutation testing (deliberately changing code to see if tests catch it) exposes weak assertions. Good coverage is necessary; coverage alone is not sufficient.

7. Maintainability of unit tests. Tests are code too. They get refactored, deleted when obsolete, and reviewed alongside production code. A 10,000-line test suite is an asset; a 10,000-line tangle of brittle, redundant tests is a liability.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Writing tests AFTER all the production code, when most of the design feedback is already lost.
  • Mocking everything — tests pass but the integrated system is broken.
  • Multi-purpose tests that fail for many reasons, making failure diagnosis slow.
  • Treating coverage targets as the goal rather than as one signal among several.

Quick recap

Unit tests give developers fast, precise feedback. TDD inverts the usual flow — write the test first, then the code — yielding testable designs and high coverage by construction. Property-based testing extends what tests can find. The tests themselves require care: they are code, with all the same maintenance considerations.

Glossary

Unit test
A fast, isolated test of a single function, method, or class.
TDD (Test-Driven Development)
Practice of writing a failing test, making it pass, then refactoring.
Mock
An object recording interactions with a dependency for verification.
Stub
An object returning canned responses to isolate a unit from its dependencies.
Property-based testing
Testing by stating properties that must hold and letting the framework generate inputs to falsify them.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — integration strategies on one system

WORKED EXAMPLE — UI → OrderService → PaymentService → DB
Units all pass alone; integration testing checks the SEAMS: does OrderService format what PaymentService expects? Does the DB transaction commit?
• Big-bang: wire everything, test at once — cheap setup, nightmare fault isolation.
• Top-down: start from the UI with stubs faking lower layers (a stub RETURNS canned answers).
• Bottom-up: start from the DB with drivers calling upward (a driver CALLS the unit under test).
• Incremental/sandwich: both ends toward the middle — the usual practical choice.
⚠️ STUB vs DRIVER
Stub = stands in BELOW you (called BY the code under test). Driver = stands in ABOVE (CALLS the code under test). Top-down needs stubs; bottom-up needs drivers. Swapping them is the classic exam distractor.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Unit tests pass but the system breaks: integration tests catch this gap. They verify that components work correctly when combined — that the database query returns what the service expects, that the API call lines up with the client, that the contract between teams holds.

Core concepts

1. What integration tests verify. Behavior across two or more components. The boundary between modules, the contract between services, the shape of data flowing across layers. Slower than unit tests, faster than full E2E, more reliable than mocks alone.

2. Integration scope choices. Sociable (real collaborators) vs solitary (mocked collaborators). Wide (many components together) vs narrow (just two). API-level vs service-internal. Each choice trades realism for stability and speed.

3. Contract testing. Specifically tests the contract between two services or modules — request/response shapes, status codes, error formats. Tools like Pact let consumer and provider verify their contract independently. Especially valuable in microservices.

4. Database integration tests. Verify that queries and migrations actually work against a real database (often a containerized Postgres or SQLite instance). Catches issues that an in-memory mock cannot — schema mismatches, transaction behaviors, real query plans.

5. External service integration. Real third-party APIs are often expensive or unreliable to call in tests. Common patterns: record-and-replay (record real calls once, replay them in tests), service stubs (fake servers returning canned responses), staging endpoints provided by the third party.

6. Test environments. Integration tests need realistic environments. Containers and infrastructure-as-code let teams spin up disposable environments per test run. Shared environments cause test interference; per-run environments are slower but reliable.

7. The middle of the test pyramid. More integration tests than E2E, fewer than unit. Each integration test costs more than a unit test but covers more. The sweet spot is enough to verify the contracts that unit tests cannot — without trying to cover every behavior that should be unit-tested.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Calling everything 'integration' — you end up with slow tests that try to cover unit-level concerns.
  • Brittle integration tests that fail intermittently due to shared state or timing.
  • Skipping contract tests in microservices, then watching consumer-provider deploys go out of sync.
  • Testing against external APIs without isolating from their availability and behavior changes.

Quick recap

Integration tests verify that components work together. They sit between unit tests (fast, isolated) and E2E tests (slow, full-stack), covering the contracts and boundaries that neither catches well. Use real dependencies where realism matters; stub when stability does.

Glossary

Integration test
A test verifying that two or more components or services interact correctly.
Contract test
An integration test specifically verifying the agreed interface between two parties.
Sociable test
An integration-style test that uses real collaborators rather than mocks.
Test container
A lightweight, ephemeral instance of a real dependency (DB, queue, etc.) used in tests.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — system & regression testing in practice

WORKED EXAMPLE — the fix that broke something else
A patch fixes rounding in the cart. System testing already validated the whole assembled product against requirements; now the patch demands regression testing: re-run the existing suite to prove old behavior still works.
And indeed: the tax test now fails — the rounding change altered tax math. That catch IS the point of regression testing.
Full suite too slow to run every commit? Select and prioritize: tests touching changed modules + critical paths first, full suite nightly — automation makes this economical, which is why regression suites are the first thing teams automate.
⚠️ REGRESSION TESTS OLD BEHAVIOR, NOT THE FIX
Testing that the fix works = re-testing/confirmation. Testing that everything ELSE still works = regression. Exams ask precisely this split.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

System testing verifies the assembled product against requirements. Regression testing verifies that yesterday's working features still work today. Together they form the safety net that lets a team change code at speed without continuously breaking what worked before.

Core concepts

1. System testing scope. Tests the integrated, complete system end-to-end against functional and non-functional requirements. Performed in an environment that resembles production. Verifies the system as a whole behaves as specified — not the parts.

2. Black-box vs white-box at the system level. System tests are usually black-box: testers exercise the system from the outside (UI, API) using only its specified interfaces, knowing nothing of internal structure. White-box system tests exist but are uncommon — at this scale, structure-based testing is unwieldy.

3. Regression testing definition. Re-running existing tests after a change to verify that previously-working behavior still works. The change might be a feature, a fix, a refactor, or a dependency upgrade. Anything could regress something.

4. Regression suite design. A regression suite grows over time. Curate it: remove obsolete tests, fix flaky ones, prioritize by risk and frequency of breakage. A 10-hour regression suite that no one runs is worse than a 30-minute suite that runs every commit.

5. Automation pays off here. Manual regression on every change is impossibly expensive at modern release cadences. The investment in automation pays off proportional to how often you ship — daily releases need automated regression; quarterly releases can lean more manual.

6. Smoke vs full regression. Smoke tests: quick verification that the build is not catastrophically broken (5-15 minutes). Full regression: thorough check of all major flows (hours). Smoke runs every deploy; full regression runs at major milestones or nightly.

7. Regression and CI/CD. In modern CI/CD, regression tests run on every pull request. Failed regression blocks merge. The team treats failures as 'must fix' rather than 'investigate later' — without that discipline, regressions accumulate and the suite stops being trusted.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Treating system tests as mere 'click-through' verification, missing real edge cases and error flows.
  • Letting the regression suite grow indefinitely until it takes hours and people skip it.
  • Tolerating flaky tests in regression — the team learns to ignore failures, missing real ones.
  • Skipping regression on 'small' changes — most regressions come from changes that 'couldn't possibly break anything'.

Quick recap

System tests verify the whole product against requirements. Regression tests verify that nothing previously working has broken. Both rely on automation at modern release cadences. Curating the regression suite — keeping it fast, reliable, and trusted — is ongoing work, not a one-time project.

Glossary

System testing
End-to-end testing of the integrated product against requirements.
Regression testing
Re-running tests after changes to verify nothing previously working has broken.
Smoke test
Quick post-build sanity check that core flows still work.
Flaky test
A test that passes and fails non-deterministically without code changes.
Test suite curation
Ongoing work to remove obsolete tests, fix flakies, and keep the suite fast and trusted.

📖 Worked example — usability & acceptance, who does what

WORKED EXAMPLE — the release’s last two gates
Usability test: five representative users are asked to “find and order blue running shoes” while observers note stumbles — 4 of 5 can’t find the size filter → a usability defect (measured by task success, time, errors, satisfaction), even though the code is “correct.”
Acceptance test (UAT): the CUSTOMER runs business scenarios against the acceptance criteria from the requirements — pass = the product is contractually done. Alpha = internal users at the dev site; beta = real users in the field.
⚠️ WHO PERFORMS IT DEFINES IT
Unit/integration/system = the team; ACCEPTANCE = the customer/end users. Black-box by nature. “Which testing is done by the client against requirements?” → UAT, final gate before sign-off.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A system that works exactly as specified can still fail users — confusing, slow, or unpleasant to use. Usability testing exposes these gaps before release. Acceptance testing confirms the system meets business needs, ending the project on shared ground rather than dispute.

Core concepts

1. Usability testing. Real users (or proxies for real users) attempt real tasks while observers watch where they hesitate, fail, or succeed. Goal: identify confusing UX, missing affordances, error states, and labels that mislead. Five users typically uncover ~80% of usability issues per round.

2. Methods of usability testing. Moderated (researcher present, can ask follow-ups). Unmoderated (user records themselves doing tasks). Remote (across distance, scales easily). In-lab (controlled conditions). A/B (real users on two versions, measure outcomes). Each suits different stages and budgets.

3. Accessibility testing. Verifies the product works for users with disabilities — screen readers, keyboard-only, color contrast, captioning. WCAG 2.1 AA is the common target; legal in many jurisdictions. Automated tools catch ~30%; manual testing finds the rest.

4. User Acceptance Testing (UAT). Business users (or their representatives) verify the system meets the business need. Performed in a near-production environment with realistic data. Often the formal sign-off step before release. The team's last chance to learn that something was misunderstood.

5. Alpha and beta testing. Alpha: early users test inside the org. Beta: real external users use a near-final build. Both surface issues that internal testing misses — real workflows, real data, real environments. Beta programs are also marketing, recruiting early advocates.

6. Acceptance criteria revisited. The acceptance criteria written with each requirement become the test cases of acceptance testing. If they were vague, acceptance testing reveals it now — too late. Discipline at requirements time pays off here.

7. When to test usability. Early prototypes (before code), wireframes (paper if needed), beta builds, and post-release. Each stage catches different issues. Earliest is cheapest; later catches what the early phase missed about real workflows.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Skipping usability testing because 'we know what users want' — almost never true.
  • Treating accessibility as a nice-to-have rather than a core requirement (often legally required).
  • Letting UAT happen on a shaky environment where most failures are environment issues, not product issues.
  • Recruiting only friendly internal users for 'usability testing' — they will not tell you the truth.

Quick recap

Usability testing surfaces UX issues with real users; accessibility testing extends quality to users with disabilities; acceptance testing confirms business needs are met. Each is a distinct activity with its own methods. All are easier and cheaper the earlier they happen.

Glossary

Usability testing
Observation of users performing tasks to identify UX issues.
Accessibility testing
Testing whether the product is usable by people with disabilities (WCAG).
UAT (User Acceptance Testing)
Formal verification by business users that the system meets requirements.
Beta test
Pre-release use by real external users to surface issues before launch.
A/B test
Comparing two versions in production with real users to measure relative performance.

UAT in the Endothon scenario: user acceptance testing means the ACTUAL end users — the loan officers — test the fixed retrieval feature against their real workflow. Passing internal QA is not acceptance; the users who felt the problem confirm it is gone.
